stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Collagraphy is a printmaking method in which textured materials are glued onto a board, inked, and pressed onto paper. It has often been treated as a classroom exercise rather than a serious medium. Yet Brazilian artist Tereza Moraes has built a three-decade career around it. Moraes layers fishing net, sand, and torn cardboard onto her plates, producing prints whose ridges can be felt as well as seen. Because the fragile surfaces wear down after five or six impressions, her editions are unusually small, and collectors now seek them out.
choices: To explain why Moraes's collagraph plates wear down after only five or six impressions
To introduce an artist who has built a serious career on a method often seen as elementary
To argue that art schools should teach collagraphy instead of more traditional printmaking methods
To contrast the materials Moraes uses with those favored by earlier collagraph artists
explanation: Every sentence serves one profile. The text defines collagraphy, notes that people often treat it as a classroom exercise, and then turns with 'Yet' to Moraes, whose long career, distinctive plates, and sought-after editions show the method used seriously. Choice B covers that whole arc, and 'introduce' matches the text's neutral, informative tone.

A.why: You picked a true detail. The plates do wear down quickly, but that is one supporting fact in a text about Moraes and her career, not the purpose of the whole passage.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text never recommends anything to art schools. It describes an artist and does not argue for a change in curriculum.

D.why: You brought in a comparison the text doesn't make. No earlier collagraph artists are mentioned, so the text cannot be contrasting Moraes's materials with theirs.

rated_why: Main point lies in overcoming low expectations of the medium itself

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Hydrologists call a river a "losing stream" when it feeds water into the ground beneath it instead of drawing water from it. Streams are not fixed in one category, though: a stream can shift between gaining and losing as the water table around it rises and falls. The Arroyo Pinto in northern Mexico is a case in point. During the summer rains, groundwater near its channel sits high enough to seep into the stream. By late winter, the surrounding aquifer has dropped so far that the arroyo's water drains downward, and the channel runs dry within a few kilometers.
choices: To explain a hydrological category and show how a single stream can move in and out of it
To describe the summer rains that raise groundwater levels near the Arroyo Pinto each year
To argue that losing streams are more vulnerable to drought than hydrologists have assumed
To show that the Arroyo Pinto remains a losing stream during every season of the year
explanation: The text defines a 'losing stream,' states the general rule that streams can switch between gaining and losing, and then uses the Arroyo Pinto to illustrate that rule. Choice A covers the definition, the rule, and the example together.

B.why: You chose one real detail. The summer rains appear only as part of the example, and the text is about the stream's changing relationship to groundwater, not about the rains.

C.why: You read in an argument the text never makes. It says nothing about drought vulnerability or about what hydrologists have wrongly assumed. It only explains and illustrates.

D.why: You reversed the example. In summer, groundwater seeps into the Arroyo Pinto, so it is gaining then. It becomes a losing stream only in late winter.

rated_why: Clear definition plus straightforward example with easily eliminated alternatives

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, the fossil plant Velatophyllum, known only from scattered leaf impressions in Antarctic rock, was assumed to be a fern. However, specimens recovered in 2019 preserve small seeds attached to the leaf bases, and ferns reproduce by spores, not seeds. Those seeds have thick protective coats, and the plant's leaves grew in tight, leathery clusters. Together, these features have led paleobotanists to reclassify Velatophyllum as an early seed plant, one apparently suited to surviving long, dark polar winters.
choices: To explain why ferns reproduce by spores rather than by producing seeds on their leaves
To argue that most plant fossils found in Antarctica have been misidentified by researchers
To describe how new specimens changed scientists' view of what kind of plant a fossil was
To show that the 2019 specimens confirmed that Velatophyllum was an unusual kind of fern
explanation: The text opens with a long-held assumption that Velatophyllum was a fern, turns on 'However' to the 2019 seed-bearing specimens, and ends with the plant's reclassification. Choice C covers that old-view-to-new-view structure for the fossil as a whole.

A.why: You picked a supporting fact. The point about spores is there only to show why seeds rule out a fern. It is a step in the reasoning, not the text's purpose.

B.why: You generalized beyond the text. It discusses one misidentified fossil and says nothing about most Antarctic plant fossils, and it doesn't argue a broad claim.

D.why: You reversed the outcome. The 2019 specimens overturned the fern classification rather than confirming it, and Velatophyllum was reclassified as a seed plant.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Metallic glasses are alloys cooled so quickly that their atoms freeze in a disordered arrangement instead of forming crystals, which makes them unusually strong and springy. For decades, however, they could be produced only as thin ribbons or small pieces, because thicker samples cooled too slowly at their centers and crystallized. Engineer Hana Okafor's team has now developed an iron-based alloy that stays glassy at thicknesses of several centimeters. Its first commercial use, in springs for precision watches, exploits the material's ability to flex millions of times without permanently deforming.
choices: To explain why rapid cooling keeps the atoms in certain alloys from arranging into crystals
To argue that metallic glasses will soon replace steel in most kinds of industrial manufacturing
To show that metallic glasses are weaker than ordinary metals but far more flexible than them
To describe a class of materials, a long-standing obstacle to making them, and a recent advance
explanation: The text moves in three steps. It says what metallic glasses are, then explains why they long couldn't be made thick ('however'), then presents Okafor's alloy and its first use. Choice D names those three parts in the order the text gives them.

A.why: You chose a true detail from the opening sentence. Rapid cooling is part of the definition, but the text goes on to cover a manufacturing limit and a breakthrough, which this choice leaves out.

B.why: You chose a verb and a claim that are too strong. The text mentions a single use in watch springs and makes no prediction about replacing steel.

C.why: You misread the properties. The text calls metallic glasses 'unusually strong,' not weaker than ordinary metals.

rated_why: Three structural concepts (definition/obstacle/solution) must be tracked and connected

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: City planners usually treat alleys as service corridors, places for trash bins and delivery trucks rather than for people. Kellbrook's Green Alley Program, launched in 2012, takes a different view. The program replaces cracked asphalt with permeable pavers that let rainwater soak into the soil, adds lighting and planters, and invites residents on each block to vote on features such as benches or murals. More than ninety of the city's alleys have now been converted, and several host weekend markets.
choices: To explain how permeable pavers reduce the amount of rainwater that flows into city drains
To describe a city program that treats alleys as public spaces rather than as service routes
To argue that other cities should adopt Kellbrook's approach to redesigning their alleys
To show that Kellbrook's alleys are still used mainly for trash collection and deliveries
explanation: After a brief note on how alleys are usually treated, the rest of the text describes the Green Alley Program: what it changes, how residents take part, and what has come of it. Choice B covers the whole text, and 'describe' fits its informative tone.

A.why: You picked a single feature. Permeable pavers are one element of the program, and the text doesn't explain drainage in any detail. It is profiling the program as a whole.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text reports what Kellbrook has done but never recommends the program to other cities.

D.why: You reversed the text. It describes how the program moved alleys away from purely service use, noting that ninety have been converted and some now host markets.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Musicologists long regarded the Ferrand Songbook, a manuscript of forty-eight part-songs from the 1590s, as the careful work of a single copyist. Close study of its ink and handwriting, however, has revealed at least four different hands. Several songs also appear twice, the second version apparently corrected after being performed. Scholars now describe the songbook not as a finished anthology but as a working collection, added to and revised by a circle of musicians over perhaps two decades.
choices: To explain how the study of ink and handwriting helps scholars date musical manuscripts
To argue that the Ferrand Songbook is the most important surviving set of 1590s part-songs
To describe how scholars have come to see a manuscript as a shared and evolving collection
To show that the Ferrand Songbook's songs were copied once and never revised afterward
explanation: The text presents the old view of the songbook as one copyist's work, turns on 'however' to the evidence of several hands and revised songs, and ends with the new view of a collaborative working collection. Choice C covers that whole shift.

A.why: You focused on the method rather than the subject. The ink and handwriting study is mentioned only as the source of the new evidence, and the text never discusses dating manuscripts.

B.why: You chose a claim the text never makes. It doesn't rank the songbook against other collections or argue for its importance.

D.why: You reversed the evidence. The text says several songs appear in a second, corrected version and that the collection was revised over decades.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: In some languages, a speaker cannot simply report that something happened; the grammar itself requires the speaker to indicate how they know it. Linguists call this feature evidentiality. In Tamuri, a language spoken by about 12,000 people in the Andean highlands, one verb suffix marks events the speaker witnessed, another marks events learned from others, and a third marks conclusions drawn from clues, such as wet ground indicating rain. Leaving the suffix off is not an option: a Tamuri sentence without one is ungrammatical.
choices: To describe a grammatical feature and illustrate it with a language that requires its use
To explain how Tamuri speakers conclude from wet ground that rain must have fallen
To argue that languages with evidentiality let speakers communicate more accurately
To show that Tamuri speakers may decide for themselves whether to mark their sources
explanation: The text begins with a general statement that some grammars require speakers to mark how they know something, names that feature evidentiality, and then uses Tamuri's three suffixes as a concrete example. Choice A covers both the general feature and the illustration.

B.why: You picked the most vivid detail. The wet-ground example only illustrates one of Tamuri's three suffixes and is not what the text as a whole is about.

C.why: You took a verb that is too strong. The text explains the feature neutrally and never claims it makes communication more accurate.

D.why: You missed the final sentence. It says leaving the suffix off is 'not an option,' so marking the source is required, not optional.

rated_why: Definition and implementation of required linguistic feature are clearly presented

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Surviving weavers' pattern books usually preserve textile designs but reveal little about the people who made them. The notebooks of Scottish weaver Janet Rennick (1821–1894) are an exception. Alongside samples of her checked woolens, Rennick recorded the price of each batch of yarn, the names of the neighbors who spun it, and the days her loom stood idle when dye shipments ran late. Historians have used the notebooks to reconstruct how a rural weaving household earned and lost money as factory cloth flooded local markets.
choices: To describe the checked woolen patterns that Rennick wove for customers in her village
To argue that the spread of factory cloth drove rural weaving households into poverty
To show that Rennick's notebooks, like most pattern books, contain only design samples
To describe a weaver's records and explain why they are valuable to historians of work
explanation: The text contrasts typical pattern books with Rennick's notebooks, lists what she recorded beyond designs, and ends with how historians have used those records. Choice D covers both what the notebooks contain and why they matter.

A.why: You chose a detail that really is in the text but is too narrow. The woolen samples are mentioned in passing, and the text's interest is in the business records kept alongside them.

B.why: You went beyond the text. It says the notebooks show how one household earned and lost money, and it doesn't argue that factory cloth impoverished rural weavers in general.

C.why: You reversed the text's central contrast. The notebooks are called 'an exception' because they record far more than designs.
